title: How Spies Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explore how spies work, opening with a discussion of Chevy Chase and the film Fletch, then the real-life Christopher Boyce and Andrew Lee case (The Falcon and the Snowman). They cover how spies are recruited (money, blackmail, ideology, walk-ins), handling through controllers and compartmentalization, dead drops, cover and legends, and tradecraft such as microfilm and photographing documents. Tools are discussed from laser microphones and satellites to spy planes, drones, undersea cable taps, and invisible ink. Historical topics include the Spartan skytale, Enigma and Bletchley Park, numbers stations, modern espionage targets (counterterrorism, China cyber attacks, corporate spying), data analysis and the Battle of Midway's Purple Code ruse, double and triple agents, Operation Fortitude and the Garbo deception before D-Day, and the Daily Telegraph crossword that hinted at D-Day code names. The episode closes with housekeeping: a new email address, a newsletter, a South by Southwest live show, and corrections about polar bears, penguins and Edmonton/Calgary.
topics: Daily Telegraph crossword D-Day code names

segments.title: Opening banter: Chevy Chase, Fletch, and The Falcon and the Snowman
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck chat about Chevy Chase, the movie Fletch, and the true story of Christopher Boyce and Andrew Lee, who sold US secrets to the Soviets in the 1970s.

segments.title: Recruiting spies
segments.summary: The hosts describe how spies are recruited: joining intelligence agencies, diplomats who spy, money, blackmail, ideological disillusionment, mother's medical bills, targeting low-level employees with access, and walk-ins such as Penkovsky.

segments.title: Controllers, compartmentalization, and dead drops
segments.summary: A spy is handled by one controller to limit exposure if caught, a practice called compartmentalization. Information is passed through dead drops in public places, with microfilm hidden in spots like a loose brick.

segments.title: Cover stories, legends, and tradecraft
segments.summary: Spies build a cover identity and a detailed backstory called a legend, which takes years to establish. Agents photograph documents rather than memorize them or steal originals, and female spies are also discussed.

segments.title: Spy gadgets and technology
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the laser EMACS device that reads vibrations on windows, noting it dates to the 1960s and is sold to the public. They discuss how modern gadgets are faster and smaller versions of older ones.

segments.title: Technical intelligence: satellites, spy planes, drones, and undersea taps
segments.summary: Technological intelligence (TECHINT) covers satellites that once dropped film canisters into the ocean and later relayed images wirelessly, U-2 spy planes replaced by drones, seismic and underwater sensors, and US submarines tapping Soviet undersea cables.

segments.title: Historical codes and secret writing
segments.summary: Ancient and historic spy methods: Sun Tzu's Art of War references to spies, invisible ink such as lemon juice and Jay's sympathetic stain in the Revolutionary War, and the Spartan skytale cipher.

segments.title: Enigma machine and Bletchley Park codebreaking
segments.summary: The German Enigma machine encrypted messages, and Polish and British codebreakers, including Alan Turing at Bletchley Park, cracked it. The book Enigma is recommended.

segments.title: Numbers stations
segments.summary: Government shortwave numbers stations broadcast coded messages, marked by a song or announcement, that anyone can hear but few can decode.

segments.title: Modern espionage: counterterrorism, cyber attacks, and corporate spying
segments.summary: Modern spying targets terror cells, Iran, North Korea, and China, with thousands of daily cyber attacks from Beijing reported. The US also spies on allies like Israel. Corporate spying during mergers and deals is described, including CIA officers moonlighting for companies and the Coke and Pepsi secret formula incident.

segments.title: Data analysis and the Battle of Midway ruse
segments.summary: Intelligence from many sources is compiled by data analysts into briefs. Stalin ignored warnings of a German attack. The Purple Code and a fake fresh-water message helped confirm the attack on Midway.

segments.title: Misinformation, double and triple agents
segments.summary: Misinformation is as important as real intelligence. Double agents may be unwitting or turned, and triple and quadruple agents make histories hard to untangle.

segments.title: Operation Fortitude and D-Day deception
segments.summary: Operation Fortitude used fake troops, tanks, depots, and a fake First US Army Group led by Patton, plus double agent Garbo and radar-reflecting chaff, to make Germany expect an invasion at Pas de Calais rather than Normandy. The hosts compare it to Blazing Saddles and discuss Saving Private Ryan.

segments.title: Daily Telegraph crossword and D-Day code names
segments.summary: MI5 noticed Daily Telegraph crossword answers such as Utah, Omaha, Mulberry, Neptune, and Overlord before D-Day. Investigation found a schoolteacher setter whose coincidence was innocent.

segments.title: Housekeeping and announcements
segments.summary: The hosts announce a new Discovery email address, a newsletter, and a South by Southwest live podcast on March 11, and ask for spy stories.

segments.title: Corrections: polar bears, penguins, and Edmonton
segments.summary: Corrections about penguins living outside Antarctica, and confusion between Edmonton and Calgary in Alberta, Canada.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Closing reminders to contact the show on Twitter, Facebook, and email, and information about the HowStuffWorks site and iPhone app.
